newsitem.title: UK: TABLE TENNIS-WALDNER ENJOYS RETURN TO THE TOP.
newsitem.headline: TABLE TENNIS-WALDNER ENJOYS RETURN TO THE TOP.

text.p: To some it's tough at the top but to Sweden's newly-crowned world table tennis champion Jan-Ove Waldner that's the only place to be.
Waldner, a near veteran at 31 years old, went through the tournament without dropping a set in regaining the title he first held in 1989.
His 21-12 21-17 21-13 triumph in Monday's final against 21-year-old Belarus star Vladimir Samsonov was the best performance of his career, according to coach Ulf Carlsson.
"It was the perfect way to play him. It was kind of a knockout victory in the second round," said Carlsson who has been a close witness to Waldner's successes over the years.

His record for eight world championships is a model of consistency. In addition to two titles, he has been runner-up twice and a losing semifinalist. Other successes include a gold medal at the 1992 Barcelona Olympics, the World Cup trophy and he is also the current European champion.
Asked how he remained motivated, he said: "It is easy for me. I am in the top now. All the time in the first five in the rankings.
"Compare me with some of the other players who are slipping in the ranks, perhaps they feel they cannot win the big titles. If this happens to me I will stop."
The Swede said that from the quarter-final onwards, he felt he could recapture the title.
"I was playing well, my touch was very good. I thought there was a chance but never to win all the matches 3-0 like this. I never believed it."
Waldner, a master tactician, knew he had to go for the quick kill against world number four Samsonov.
"I had to be aggressive. Vlad is very strong, hitting backhand and forehand, so its very tough to beat him in the long rallies. You have to play aggressive to him, one serve and kill."
The Swede said the second set had been crucial.
"He was pressing very hard. It was very important for me and Vlad mentally. After the second set, I knew I had a good chance to win."
Waldner had played two five-set double matches earlier on Monday - he and Jorgen Persson lost in the final to two Chinese - and he was concerned about his stamina.
"Vlad was probably more fresh than me and if he had won the second set and it went to a fifth, he would have been the favourite."
"This was his first big final. He'll probably win his next one," Waldner said.
For Waldner, it was too early to contemplate his next target. "The first thing to do now is to celebrate," he laughed.
